title: OOP Fundamentals: Classes, Objects, and Attributes
description: Defining classes, creating objects, constructors, and the distinction between instance and class members.
objectives: Define a class with a constructor and instance methods
Understand self and how instance attributes work
Distinguish instance variables, class variables, instance methods, class methods, and static methods
Apply basic encapsulation with naming conventions

content.heading: Classes, Objects, and __init__
content.body:
A class is a blueprint for creating objects; class ClassName: introduces one. __init__(self, ...), the constructor, runs automatically when you create a new object with ClassName(...), and is where you typically set up instance attributes — data that belongs to that specific object. self is the first parameter of every instance method and refers to the particular object the method was called on; Python passes it automatically (obj.method(x) is really ClassName.method(obj, x) under the hood). Attributes are accessed and set with dot notation: obj.attribute.

Encapsulation in Python is convention-based rather than enforced by the language: a single leading underscore (_name) signals 'internal use, please don't touch from outside', and a double leading underscore (__name) triggers name mangling (renamed internally to _ClassName__name), making accidental external access harder but not impossible. There is no true private keyword like Java's private.

content.heading: Instance vs. Class Members
content.body:
Instance variables (set via self.x = ...) belong to one specific object; each object has its own independent copy. Class variables (defined directly in the class body, outside any method) are shared by every instance of the class — useful for constants or counters that should be common to all instances, but a frequent source of bugs if a mutable class variable is accidentally shared when independent instance-level data was intended.

Instance methods (def method(self):) operate on a specific object and can read/modify its attributes. Class methods (@classmethod, taking cls instead of self) operate on the class itself, often used as alternative constructors. Static methods (@staticmethod, taking neither self nor cls) are just regular functions logically grouped inside the class namespace, with no access to instance or class state.

content.explanation: self.balance is unique per account object, while bank_name is shared class-wide. zero_balance() is a classmethod used as an alternative way to construct a BankAccount.

keyPoints: __init__ is the constructor; self refers to the specific instance a method was called on
Instance variables belong to one object; class variables are shared across all instances
@classmethod methods receive the class (cls); @staticmethod methods receive neither self nor cls
Python encapsulation is convention-based (_name, __name) rather than enforced by a private keyword
commonMistakes: Forgetting the self parameter in an instance method definition
Using a mutable class variable (like a list) when each instance actually needed its own independent copy
